intro: Buddhist texts reached English readers only in the 1800s. Translators at Oxford and London, monks in Sri Lanka and Burma, and teachers from Japan all played a part. In 1893, Buddhist speakers stood before a crowd in Chicago. In this unit, you will follow how Buddhist texts and teachers came to America.

You will meet Max Müller, the Rhys Davids, Edwin Arnold, Anagarika Dharmapala, Soyen Shaku and D.T. Suzuki, who once lived in La Salle, Illinois. Then you will follow Japanese American Buddhists through the wartime camps to new temples in Chicago in 1944, and see the immigrant temples, convert centers and mindfulness debates of today.

By the end, you will be able to explain how translators' word choices shape meaning, describe the 1893 Parliament and its Buddhist speakers, tell the story of Japanese American Buddhism and Chicago's temples, and discuss questions American Buddhists face today.
bigQuestion: How did Buddhist texts and communities come to America, and how have they been translated, kept and changed?

Jon Kabat-Zinn starts Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction
U.S. government apologizes for the incarceration
The Dalai Lama receives the Nobel Peace Prize
